turns.reply:
The road finds company before the walls do. A carter's mule train creaks up from the south, four wagons deep with early apples, and a file of pilgrims in grey travel weeds walks at the shoulder of the road with their hoods back, singing something with a river in it. Their feet have raised a pale dust that hangs in the morning light long after they pass. The wind carries crushed apple, mule dung, woodsmoke from somewhere beyond the fields.

Lumenford's west gate grows as the road bends — two drum towers, a chain hoisted and rusted at the peak, the arch beneath dark with traffic. A wooden board nailed beside the arch lists tolls in a clerk's careful hand: cart, two coppers. Beast of burden, one copper. Foot traveler, free.

A short queue has formed at the arch. A man in a quilted jack leans against the stonework with a boar-spear resting against his shoulder, waving most of the traffic through with two fingers. His partner, older, grey at the temples, takes the tolls from the carters and marks a slate. Neither of them looks up when the pilgrims file past — the singers get a nod, nothing more. The carter at the front is arguing about his axle.

"Third time this month, Osper. I'm not carrying your axle through my gate."

"It held from Ashbridge, didn't it? Held the whole river road."

"It held. Past tense. Fix it or walk your fruit in by the basket."

The carter swears at the sky, then at the mule, then pays his two coppers, and the wagons roll under the arch with a sound like slow thunder. The queue moves up. Somewhere inside the walls a bell rings the third hour, flat and unhurried, and a gull screams over the towers — the river must run close on the far side.

The man with the boar-spear straightens off the wall as the next place in the queue comes up. He gives Alaric's bow a glance, the kind men give a tool rather than a threat, then holds out a flat palm — not for coin, the board was plain enough — and tips his chin toward the arch.

"Quills out, staves stay shouldered, no fights inside the first street. Temple wardens take it serious this month, pilgrimage season." He jerks his thumb at the grey-hooded singers, already swallowed by the arch. "Thirty of them yesterday, forty today. Everybody's a saint until somebody's purse goes walking."

He steps aside, waving him toward the dark of the gateway, where the queue from the north side is already funneling through a smell of wet stone and old horse.

"—fresh eels, river eels, caught this morning, woman, I don't smoke them I sell them—" A fishmonger's barrow has jammed itself against the gate's inner shadow, and the first street beyond the arch is already a river of its own: barrows, mules, a woman hauling wicker creels, two grey-hooded pilgrims kneeling to kiss the threshold stone while the traffic splits around them with practiced annoyance.

The city smells of wet stone and frying onions and, under it, the river. Carts grind past on cobble worn slick down the middle. A bell somewhere counts the quarter hour wrong, or the first bell counted it wrong; nobody on the street seems to care.

Wayfinding offers itself. Armed folk drift here like iron filings — a woman with a boar-spear across her back, a pair of men in mail shirts with crossbows slung, all of them cutting the same diagonal away from the market noise, up a street where the buildings put on stone faces. Halfway along, a timber-framed building stands with its shutters thrown wide and a sign swinging over the door: a carved bow crossed over a spear, paint gone chalky with weather. The door stands open. From inside, raised voices.

"—half the hide, half the tusks, that was the terms."

"The terms were you shot it in the arse, Drennik, after I'd bled it for an hour. The arse. You want half the tusks for an arrow in the arse."

Inside, the common room is low-beamed and loud with morning business. A long counter runs the left wall, behind it a clerk with ink-stained fingers stamping papers one after another, a queue of four before her. The right wall is papered floor to ceiling with notices — bounty bills, wax-stamped contracts, a board of torn-off stubs. In the middle of the room a scarred table hosts the argument's owners: a big man in a ring-mail shirt, Drennik presumably, and a lean older woman with grey in her braid and a boar's tusk strung on a cord at her neck. She's tapping the tabletop with one finger on every word.

At the counter, a warden in temple grey — a sword in a peace-bonded scabbard, sun-wheel stitched at the collar — is holding a notice while the clerk stamps without looking up.

"It goes center board, Serah. Not the side. The side gets buried under boar bills by noon."

"It goes where there's room, Warden. Center's for Guild-posted work."

"It's a forty-silver reward. It goes center."

He takes the hammer from her, spits a nail into his palm, and reaches up to the middle of the board. The notice, upside down for a moment before the hammer falls, is large and written in a careful temple hand: missing — two pilgrims en route from Ashbridge, last seen on the river road three days past. Information leading to their recovery, forty silver. The room's noise dips around it, then resumes, the way water resumes around a stone.

The clerk finishes her queue and looks down the counter, eyes passing over the room without hurry.

turns.input: *i walk to the Clerk* Hello im Alaric no family name and im new to the guild and want to register
turns.reply:
"Name's on the slate, not in the air." The clerk stamps a paper, sets it in a finished pile, and only then looks up — pale eyes, a ink smudge along one jaw where she's scratched at it. "Alaric, no family. Fine. Half the board's the same, the other half's lying about it."

She pulls a ledger across the counter and turns it so it faces outward, then sets a stub of black chalk in the groove beside it.

"Serah. I run the counter, the counter runs the hall. Questions in order, answer in order." Her finger comes down on the ledger, one line at a time. "Age. Class, if it's come to you yet — don't be embarrassed if it hasn't, the board's half farmhands who swear they're Warriors. Next of kin or whoever to write to when you're dead. You'd be surprised who leaves that blank."

She's already reaching under the counter for a flat slate, dark and smooth as river stone, a Guild seal carved at its head.

"Hand on the slate when I tell you. It reads what you are — Rank, nothing else. The Guild doesn't pry." A beat, and the chalk stub turns over in her fingers. "The temple pries. Different building. Ignore anyone grey-robed who asks what the slate said."

Across the room the argument breaks. Drennik comes up off the bench with the whole bench leg screeching, jabs a finger at the grey-braided huntress — "Half the hide is HALF, Maretta, you can't just—" — and she collects her boar tusk from her neck cord, kisses it once, and turns her back on him to the bar. He stands there breathing through his nose like a bull deciding, then storms for the door, shouldering past a crossbowman hard enough to stagger him, and is gone into the street. The crossbowman watches him go, says nothing, and the room settles back into its noise like a bed being made.

Serah hasn't followed any of it. Her chalk is already hovering.

"Two silver for registration. Covers the slate reading, the tag, and your first year's dues. After that it's one a year and I'll find you to collect it, which nobody wants." She sets the slate flat between them, carved seal up, and puts two fingers on its edge without pressing. "Fee first, then hand on the slate. Then you're Guild, Rank F, Novice, and the board out there is your problem instead of everybody else's."

She nods once at the papered wall, at the bounty bills and wax-stamped contracts, and her eyes come back flat and patient to the counter between them, where the two silver haven't appeared yet.

turns.reply:
The slate is cold under the palm — river-stone cold, and then not. Something crosses it from the inside, faint as a fish passing under ice, and where the carved seal sits at the head of the slate a line of pale light draws itself along the groove and settles into a single letter.

**F**

"There it is." Serah tips the two silver out of the groove where they've landed, bites one out of old habit, and drops both into a locked drawer that comes open and shut under her hand in one motion. "Eighteen, Ranger. Young for the board, old enough for it." She pulls the ledger back around and writes in a hand faster than the stamp comes down — name, age, class, Rank, a dash where next of kin would go. "Blank on kin. You'd be surprised who does that. Most of them mean to fill it in later."

She tears a tag off a strip of soft lead, stamps it twice, and slides it across the counter with one finger. A number is punched through it, and the Guild seal under the number.

"That's yours. Don't lose it, replacing it costs you, and don't sell it, which has been tried. Rule of the house is simple: take what you can kill, run from what you can't, and bring the tag back when you're done so I know whether to strike you off." A fresh queue is forming at the counter's far end; she marks a line under his entry without looking at them. "Board's on the right wall. Wax color's what matters — brown is Novice work, and brown is what you take. Anything with a red seal, leave hanging. Contracts come to me for stamping, pay comes back through me, and the Guild keeps ten of whatever you earn, which is how the lights stay on."

She glances past him at the board, and the temple notice hanging dead center.

"Forty silver on that pilgrim bill, if you're thinking it. Information only. The temple doesn't pay for bodies, it pays for answers, and the warden who posted it is in here twice a day asking who's come in off the river road." Her pale eyes come back around, flat. "Nobody has. Nobody's taken it. Two seasons back a Novice took a temple bill like it and came back with a story nobody bought."

She picks up the next stamp in the queue.

"Congratulations, Alaric, no family. Brown wax, counter, ten percent. Go be somebody's problem."

"—and take the wolf bill while you're staring at it, girl, or don't, I don't care." Maretta is already at the board when Alaric reaches it, a drink in one hand and her other hand flat on the papered wall. She pulls a brown-wax bill off its nail, reads it upside down, and puts it back. "Twenty silver for wolves and everyone acts like it's poisoned."

The Novice section hangs lowest, at chest height, brown wax stamps shining dull on maybe a dozen bills. Several are old enough to have gone honey-colored at the corners.

**WOLVES NEAR THE ASHBRIDGE FORD** — shepherds lost three lambs this week; cull or drive off; proof wanted, ears. 20 silver.

**RIVER DRAKE ON THE FISH WEIRS** — one young drake sunning itself downstream of the eel traps; drive it off, don't gut it where it breeds. 15 silver.

**VERMIN IN THE MALTHOUSE CELLAR** — something's been at the malt sacks; cats have failed. 8 silver.

**ESCORT TO MILLBROOK** — herb-woman's cart, two days out and back, leaves Day 3. 12 silver.

**PACKETS TO THE STONEBRIDGE TOLLHOUSE** — papers, sealed, walk there, walk back. 4 silver.

Maretta's finger comes down on the wolf bill, taps it twice, and she plucks it off the nail proper this time and folds it into her shirt. "Mine." She says it to the board, or the room, or nobody, and turns for the counter, draining her cup on the way. The drake bill flutters where her shoulder grazed it.

Behind Alaric, the street door swings and the room's noise dips for the second time this morning. Temple grey, sun-wheel at the collar, the same warden who hammered the notice to center board — he comes in with river mud dried gray up one boot and his eyes already working the benches.

"Morning, all." He doesn't raise his voice; he doesn't need to, the room has already gone quiet enough. "River road, this morning or last night. Carters, travelers, anyone come in off it. Two pilgrims still owing the temple an arrival." He pulls the folded notice from his belt, doesn't open it. "Forty silver still hanging. Answers, mind. Not bones."

The crossbowman by the fire shakes his head. The fish-apron boy at the counter shakes his. Maretta, halfway to Serah, doesn't shake hers — she stops, and looks at the warden, and looks at the wolf bill in her hand, and stands there weighing something while the warden's eyes keep traveling the room.

turns.reply:
"Eight silver, brown wax, vermin." Serah has the bill out of Alaric's hand before the counter, unfolds it, and finds the blank line. "Proof's whatever the employer says counts. Read your own bill — most of them want it dead, some of them just want it gone. Sign, stamp, done." The stamp comes down. "Guild's ten comes off the pay, off the top, before you start counting it as yours. Malthouse is on Eel Lane, downstream side, the building that smells like bread gone wrong."

Behind him the other business is still hanging. Maretta hasn't moved from her spot between bar and counter, and the warden has drifted over, notice still folded, patient as a post.

"You didn't shake your head, Maretta."

"I didn't shake it at anything." She sets her cup down on the counter, upside down over the drip tray. "Wolf bill, Serah. Stamp it. Ashbridge Ford, twenty silver, ears."

"Off the river road, is the Ford."

"Everything's off the river road. It's a road." She takes the tusk from her cord, kisses it, and strings it back while Serah stamps. "Prints by the ford, three shepherds short some lambs. That's my answer, warden. Count it or don't."

Ansel doesn't blink at her. He watches her a while with his eyes steady and open, the way a man watches a door he expects to open, and gets nothing for it. She takes her stamped bill, folds it in with the other, and is out the street door with her bow knocking against her back, gone toward the west gate and the ford.

"Two seasons, that one's been walking that road," the crossbowman says to the fire. Nobody answers him.

---

Eel Lane runs downhill toward the river between tannery fences and eel-smoke sheds, and the malthouse sits where the lane flattens — long, low, thatched, breathing warmth through its shuttered vents. The smell arrives before the door does: malt, wet grain, something sweeter underneath gone sour. A boy is hauling sacks onto a handcart in the yard, and a thickset man in a floury apron stands over him counting under his breath — forty-one, forty-two — and stops counting when the door creaks.

"Guild?" He looks at the tag, then the bow, then back to the tag, and his shoulders drop a half-inch like a man setting down a load he'd been holding wrong. "Fennick. This is my floor, my malt, my cellar." He wipes his hands down the apron, which moves the flour around. "Cats won't go down there anymore. That's the part I want you to sit with, lad. Cats. Won't. Go."

He leads the way through the malting floor, past turners of grain and the heat rising through the slats, to a door in the corner stones, iron-banded, closed. A bar across it. He lifts the bar and stands the door open on darkness and a smell of cellar cold and, faintly, gnawed grain.

"Started at the far sacks a month back. Small at first, I figured rats, so I laid poison. They ate the poison. Didn't die." He nods at the dark. "Gnaw marks sit this high on the sacks." His hand levels off at his own chest. "Rats don't climb to chest height and keep their manners about it."

From down the stone steps, out of the dark, something shifts — a slow drag of weight across grain, then quiet, then quiet, then quiet.

Fennick's hand finds the doorframe and stays there.

turns.reply:
Cold climbs the legs first — a cellar cold that has sat shut in a stone box for a month, carrying malt and mouse and something wetter underneath. The stairwell gives the doorway's light in slices: six steps down, a turn, six more, and the floor of the cellar is a pale spill of daylight that goes nowhere. Past its edge the dark keeps everything it has.

From the top, Fennick's voice comes down thin. "Lamp hook's on the second post, if you want light. I never took the lamp back out." A pause, and under it, barely, counting — "eight, nine sacks gone, ten—" — stopping itself like a tap twisted shut.

The bow is drawn before the last step. String at cheek, point moving with the eyes, the floor's daylight showing what the dark won't: sacks shouldered against the far wall, the near ones torn open at chest height exactly as promised, spill of malt fanned out below like something fed there standing up. A drag trail through the spill, wide as a man's forearm, leading back into the black behind the pillar.

The trail is warm. That's the detail that arrives last — the malt in it flattened and faintly greasy, fresh enough that it isn't a month old, isn't a week old. It's this morning old.

The check fails quietly. Nothing moves where the eyes are looking, because the eyes are looking at the trail and not above it, and the sound, when it comes, comes from the dark past the pillar — a click. Then a second click. Nail on stone, or tooth on stone, and close.

"Lad." Fennick, at the top of the stairs, flat and careful. "Lad, that's no rat."

The dark gives up its shape in pieces. Low along the floor at first — then it isn't low, it's climbing the sacks, up to the torn chest height, and the light from the stairwell finds two eyes set close together and wet-looking, and a head too big for the body under it, and a mouth already open. It comes off the sacks in a long gray leap.

The arrow takes the leap full in the chest — and takes it wrong. Too much bow for the distance, the point drives through where the body should have been and finds only the follow-through of the jump, and the shaft glances off the sack-wall behind it with a sound like a knuckle cracking. The creature lands short, on the spill of malt, and its claws skid grain in both directions.

It's built wrong for anything Fennick keeps cats for. Long as a forearm, grey, wet-eyed, the oversized head all mouth — teeth in rows meant for holding, and it uses them. It comes up off the grain fast, inside the arrow's arc before the string has gone quiet, and its jaw closes on the meat of the forearm above the bracer.

Three points of it go in. The pull-back is worse than the bite — teeth meant to hold tear on the way out — and then it's off again, dropping to all fours between Alaric and the stairs, chewing the mouthful it stole. Swallowing. Not running. The eyes stay fixed the whole time, wet and close-set, and it sways its head side to side like a snake tasting where the next bite lives.

Blood runs warm under the bracer's edge and drips off two fingers. The malt under it is dark and damp for a hand's width around.

"That's it eating you, lad." Fennick, from the top of the stairs, voice pinched to a thread. "That's what's been down here a month. EIGHT silver, that bill said—"

The creature's hind legs gather.

The string snaps and the arrow goes over — the thing springs low instead of high this time, belly to the grain, and the shaft buries itself in a sack behind it with a soft gush of malt. Twelve silver of bow, spent on a shape the eye keeps misjudging.

The ground it gains back is worse than the miss. It doesn't sprint; it flows, a long gray ripple across the cellar floor, and the half-step of retreat is gone before the back foot finds its place. Teeth close on the thigh — through trouser, through the light armor's edge, three points in, three points out. Warmth spreads down the leg and starts ticking off the boot onto the stone.

"Two." Fennick, at the top of the stairs, breath short. "That's two bites. Two bites is — lad, the stairs, get your back to the—"

The creature swallows. It does this every time, unhurried, eyes never leaving him, and between swallows it moves — sideways now, a short shuffle along the arc of the daylight, and the shuffle ends with it sitting square in the line between the cellar floor and the bottom step. Not crouched. Sitting. Like a thing that has decided where the next bite comes from and is willing to wait for the arm to tire.

Above, Fennick has stopped pretending not to count. "One bow. One hunter. Eight silver, forty sacks of malt, one cellar—" The counting cuts off. In the quiet after it, from the black behind the pillar, the second click comes again. Nail on stone.

And something answers it. From deeper in the dark, past the far sacks, a second voice — same click, lower, twice the size of the sound.

The grey thing's head turns toward it. For the first time since the leap, its eyes leave him.

"Third one. Lad, that's three—"

The bow answers before the complaint does. The grey thing has its head still turned toward the dark behind the pillar when the string goes, and at the sound it jerks — not away, toward, a flinch into the click like a dog hearing its name — and the shaft passes through where its skull was and splits against the stone pillar in a spray of splinters and malt dust.

Then it's on him.

No leap this time. It's already too close for one; it simply rises off its haunches and its mouth finds the outside of the calf, above the boot's collar, three points in and dragged out sideways on the retreat. The leg buckles a half-inch and holds. Warmth runs inside the boot now, joining the tick of blood off the fingers, and the floor's daylight spill is getting crowded with dark drops.

The creature backs off two body-lengths and swallows. Longer this time — a bigger mouthful, the throat working and working — and when it finishes, its head swings back toward the stairs, back to its sitting place on the line, and its hind legs are already under it again. Swaying. Wet eyes, close-set, fixed.

Behind the far sacks the deeper click has stopped clicking. Something back there is moving instead — a slow, wide displacement of grain, sacks shifting their shoulders in the dark, a weight finding its feet. The grey one's ears — flat, leathery, easy to miss — have swiveled toward it and stayed there.

"Lad." Fennick's voice has gone to almost nothing, and under it the counting has started again, faster, barely shaped as numbers. "There's two. Lad, there's always been two."

The jump buys a body-length and the bow buys the rest. The arrow goes past the grey thing's swaying head — into the dark where the weight is — and the grey thing leaps straight into the arrow's road, chasing the shot the way it chased the clicks, and the point takes it through the open mouth and out the back of the too-big skull.

It hits the malt spill rolling, thrashes once against the sacked wall, and is still. The legs go stiff, then loose. The wet eyes stay open, fixed on nothing.

"Is it dead. Lad, is it dead, is it—" Fennick, at the top of the stairs, and under his words the counting has come all the way out now, fast, "—one, one bow, one dead, that's one—"

Behind the far sacks, the weight answers before Alaric can.

Not toward the light. Away from it. The grain drags in a long slow pull, sacks settling their shoulders, the sound of something heavy deciding against — and it goes deep, deeper than the sacks, down toward the floor's far corner where the stones sit older and darker. There's a gap down there. The sound says so. A gap at the base of the foundation wall, wide enough for a body that has been coming and going through it for a month, and the dragging narrows, and thins, and stops being a sound at all. The cellar goes back to what it was: cold, malt-sour, and quiet.

"Lad." Fennick's face has come down two steps into the light, flour-white against the dark behind him, and he's looking past the dead grey thing to the far corner. He knows the corner. His mouth does something with the knowing and doesn't manage a word for it, and then he does. "There's a drain under there. Old river drain. My father's father bricked it shut, and the bricks—" His hand wipes down the apron. "The bricks are somebody else's problem. Get up these stairs. Bring that thing with you, I'm not paying eight silver on trust and a bleeding boy."

He stands there gripping the doorframe, waiting, and from the top of the stairs his eyes never once go to the dark corner. They go to the body. To the arrow in it. To the count of silver that's about to leave his purse.

"Mind the first step. It's loose. Been loose for years."

turns.reply:
The corpse comes up the stairs lighter than it looks — most of the weight is in that wrong big head, and the dead don't fight the loose first step the way a live man would. Fennick meets it at the top with a grain shovel held out like he doesn't want his hands on it, and together they get the thing onto the shovel and lay it out on the malting floor slats, where the turners stop their rakes and crowd in at a distance nobody could call respectful.

"Teeth." Fennick crouches over the head without touching it, and his eyes go to the creature's open ones and stay there a beat too long — a man checking a memory against the original. Then he's up and brushing his knees, brisk, done. "Three silver now."

"Three? The bill says—"

"The bill says something's been at the sacks, and something HAS been, and one of the somethings is dead." He's already counting coins out of the apron pocket, under his breath, three, and six coppers, and his thumb stops on a fourth silver and moves off it like it's hot. "There's one still in my wall, lad. In my WALL. Five more when it's dead and the drain's bricked. That's fair. That's more than fair, that's— you bit. Look at you. You're dripping on my floor." He presses the coins into a fold of cloth held out like a scoop, not touching the hand. "Barber on this lane, past the smoke sheds, left side. Two coppers a wound and he sews crooked, but he sews. Go before it goes bad."

The coins are warm from his pocket. At the door he's already turned back to the cellar stairs, and he sets the bar across it standing up in its brackets, ready to drop, before the yard gate has finished swinging.

---

The Guild hall at mid-morning has changed its weather. The argument table is empty, the wolf bill's nail holds only a torn stub, and two men in eel-sellers' aprons stand at the notice wall reading the drake bill aloud to each other, one of them tapping the fifteen silver with a finger gone scarred white at the knuckle. Somebody's dog is asleep against the cold hearth. The smell of the morning's first drink has settled into the room along with sawdust and wet wool.

Serah sees the blood before she sees the bill. Her eyes go down the sleeve, down the leg, one pass, and come back up to the counter with no change in them.

"Vermin bill. And you're leaking on my counter, which is a bad start to a settlement." She takes the brown-wax paper, unfolds it, finds the line. "State of it. Dead, gone, or partly?"

The stamp waits in her hand. Behind her, the locked drawer that opened for two silver this morning sits shut, and at the far end of the counter a queue of three is forming — the eel-sellers have changed their minds about the drake.

"Because if it's partly, the bill stays on the board and the wax stays brown, and Fennick decides what half a job buys. He'll have told you already, if you've just come from him. That man counts his own blinks."

"Partly." Serah sets the stamp down without using it and pulls the bill flat on the counter, reading it again end to end like it might have changed since this morning. "One dead, one fled. Fennick paid you under half." A grunt that could pass for agreement. "That's Fennick. The bill was for the cellar, the cellar's still got something in it, so the bill stays live."

She takes up a pencil stub, licks the point, and writes in the margin in a hand small enough to fit a month of names on a thumbnail: *one killed, one withdrawn — balance 5 silver on second kill, drain stopped.* Then she blows on it, folds it, and slides it back across the counter.

"Your paper now. Keep it. His promise is worth what his word's worth, which is nothing with a ledger behind it, and this is the ledger." Her palm comes out flat over the counter's groove. "Guild's ten. Off the top. Three and six is thirty-six copper, so it's four — I don't cut copper into eighths, and rounding down is a habit for people who die poor."

The four coppers disappear into the locked drawer.

"Now get off my counter and find that barber. Two coppers a wound, and you're carrying at least three from the smell of it. Come in here leaking tomorrow and I'll stamp your papers in red and let the temple ask questions." She's already reaching past him for the queue. "Next."

The eel-sellers have settled it between themselves while the counter was busy. The older one — the scarred-knuckle finger — has the drake bill off its nail and is reading it aloud for the third time, slow, the way a man reads a price he means to argue with. The younger one, broad through the chest with forearms smoked yellow to the elbow, is shaking his head at every line.

"Fifteen silver, and it says drive off. Drive off. I'm not rowing out there to wave a pole at a drake, Tam, I'm saying we spear it and sell it."

"It says don't gut it where it breeds. It doesn't say don't gut it."

"That's the weirs' breeding water, you old — that's the SAME water—"

"Then you'll want a hunter with a bow, won't you." Serah, over both of them, stamp hand lifted. "Or you'll want the next in the queue, which is nobody, because you two are it. Decide."

The younger one is still looking at the wall where the bill hung, but the older one — Tam — has turned, and his eyes go from the counter to the tag, to the bow, to the blood going stiff along the sleeve, and he taps the bill with the white-scarred finger twice, the same way he tapped the fifteen silver.

"Vermin's one thing," he says. "A drake's got teeth on the end of it. You bite back, boy?"

Maretta turns on the counter-rail, unhurried, and gives Alaric the once-over — bow, boots, the newness of him — the way she'd look at a ewe she wasn't sure was worth the pen.

"Ford's big enough for two sets of ears." She kisses the boar tusk at her neck, brief, like a habit worn smooth. "Silver isn't. Walk fast, boy."

From a bench's length away, Warden Ansel has stopped not-blinking.

"Ashbridge Ford is river road." He says it to the space between them, low, unhurried. "If the road shows you two pilgrims — grey hoods, Ashbridge registry marks — answers, mind. Come to me before you come to the bill." He touches the folded notice at his belt once and lets it be.

---

The river road runs southwest out of Lumenford with the water on its left, and by midday the city has fallen behind to a smoke-smudge on the sky behind. Traffic thins the further out it goes — a knacker's cart, two grey hoods walking east with their sandals in their hands, a woman mending a hurdle who watches him pass twice. The tollhouse at the halfway mark has its bar up; the keeper on the stoop lifts two fingers at a foot traveler and goes back to his pipe. The river runs wide and brown-green here, patient, smelling of silt and crushed weed.

The ford announces itself before it appears — wool. A hundred sheep at least on the south bank, and a shepherd's dog working them away from the water in tight, offended arcs. Then the ford itself: a gravel spine through the shallows, stepping stones, willows crowding the far bank.

The lamb is on the near bank, twenty paces off the road in the tussock grass. Three days dead, by the smell and the crows sitting fat on it — throat opened, hindquarters gone at, wool pulled loose in mats. A shepherd has been out here since; a hazel stick stands planted beside it with a strip of red cloth tied on, a marker for a claim somebody will argue about later.

The prints around it have been rain-softened and re-hardened. Old. But crossing them, sharp-edged in the mud where a seep runs down to the water, are newer ones — long pad, four toes, a stride that means business. Three animals, moving together upriver toward the willow line.

And in that same mud, a boot print. Small, worn heel, days' worth of road in the tread. It comes off the road, stands a while at the lamb, and goes on toward the willows.

Downstream, all at once, the crows lift out of the far bank's trees.
